opus-5.5.text:
You know, one of the things that's striking is how abstract it all feels. You read that some company is going to invest this enormous sum, a number so large it's hard to even hold in your head, and then you go about your day and nothing is different. It's a headline. It doesn't touch your life. It's a bit like it's happening somewhere else.

And I think that's actually an important observation, because it tells you something about how people will process change more generally. Even very large things, if they arrive as numbers and announcements, don't register emotionally.

The economic impact, I expect, will be felt very differently. When AI really starts to do things, when it changes what your job looks like, what a company can do, how quickly things get built, people will feel it directly. It won't be an abstraction anymore. It will be in the texture of daily life.

But I'd add one nuance. Right now there is a strange disconnect. The models are really impressive on evaluations, and yet the economic impact seems to lag quite a bit behind what you'd expect from those evaluations. That gap is real, and I think it's one of the more confusing things about the current moment. It points to something about generalization: these systems can do remarkably well on a test and still not be as robust or as reliable as a person in the real-world setting.

So my expectation is something like this. For a while it continues to feel abstract: big announcements, impressive demos, and a somewhat muted effect on the economy. Then, as the systems become genuinely more capable and generalize better, the impact becomes very concrete. When that happens I don't think people will experience it the way they experience investment news. They'll experience it as the world changing around them. That's when I'd expect attitudes, including those of governments and the AI companies themselves, to shift quite a lot, because things will finally feel real.

r001.rationale: It contrasts enormous investment announcements that feel abstract and disconnected from daily life with AI’s future economic impact being directly felt in jobs, companies, and daily life.

r002.rationale: It predicts that more capable, better-generalizing systems will make AI’s impact concrete, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI’s diffusion throughout the economy.

fable-5.1.text:
So right now, when you hear about these investments — someone announces a hundred billion dollars, a trillion dollars, these enormous numbers — it's like a headline. You read it, you think, wow, that's a lot of money, and then you go on with your day. It doesn't really touch your life. The numbers are so large that they become abstract, almost like reading about astronomy.

But the economic impact, when it comes, will not be like that. It will be very concrete. It will be: my job changed. The thing I used to do is now done by a model. The company I work for is organized differently. Or it will be that something that used to be expensive is now cheap, or something that used to take a long time now takes very little time. These are things you feel directly, in your own life, not things you read about.

And I think there's a gap right now, which is that the investment is running ahead of the impact. The investment is based on a belief about what will happen. And I think the belief is correct, broadly. But the impact so far is small relative to the investment, and people notice that. They say, where is it? I see the announcements but I don't see my life changing. And I think that's an honest reaction. The models are impressive but they're not yet doing the full job in most places. There's a difference between being very good at evals and being something that a company can really hand work to and trust.

So my expectation is that the announcements will keep feeling abstract, and then at some point the impact will stop being abstract and will become very personal, and that transition will be fast once it starts, which is part of what makes it hard for people to be prepared for it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts enormous investment announcements that feel abstract and distant with economic changes—such as jobs changing or services becoming cheaper—that people will feel directly.

r002.rationale: It expects AI’s impact to become personal and arrive quickly, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI’s diffusion throughout the economy.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a difference between hearing about a very large investment and experiencing what it produces. Someone announces a hundred billion dollars, and you understand that this is a big number. But it’s still abstract. Your life the next morning is pretty much the same.

The economic impact would be much more direct. You encounter a system that can do some work you need done, and then you realize it can do a lot more of that work than you expected. It changes what your company can do, what things cost, perhaps what your own job looks like. That’s when it becomes real to people.

Of course, investment is not itself proof that this impact will happen, or tell us exactly when. But if the capabilities keep improving, people will experience the consequences through changes in their everyday lives. That will be a very different kind of understanding from reading an announcement.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a huge investment announcement as abstract, with daily life unchanged, against AI’s impact becoming real through changes to work, costs, companies, and jobs.

r002.rationale: It says improving capabilities could bring everyday consequences, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI’s diffusion throughout the economy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big difference between hearing about an investment and experiencing what that investment produces. You hear that some company is spending a hundred billion dollars, and it’s a very large number, but it’s abstract. Your life hasn’t changed as a result of hearing it.

The economic impact would be much more direct. What can you get done? What does it cost? What happens to your job, or to the business you’re running? Those are things people experience personally.

And there can be a substantial delay between the two. The investment is visible immediately, while turning the technology into something useful across the economy takes time. So I would expect people’s understanding of AI to change much more when they encounter its consequences in their own lives than when they read the announcements.

r001.rationale: It describes large investment announcements as abstract and contrasts them with people directly experiencing effects on work, costs, jobs, and businesses.

r002.rationale: It says making technology useful across the economy takes time, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI’s diffusion.
